title: Adverb Placement in Second Language Acquisition: Some Effects of Positive and Negative Evidence in the Classroom
design: Quasi-experimental classroom intervention comparing learners given form-focused instruction that included negative evidence (explicit correction on adverb placement) against learners exposed only to positive input, with immediate and delayed posttests
population: Francophone (L1 French) 11-12 year-old learners of English as a second language in core-French/ESL classrooms in Quebec, Canada
topic: focused L2 instruction and form-focused instruction
outcome: Learners who received form-focused instruction including negative evidence on English adverb placement outperformed learners given only positive input, on both immediate and delayed posttests of correct adverb placement.
limitations: Instruction was delivered to intact classes rather than individually randomized learners, and some delayed-posttest gains partially receded, limiting claims about durability.
qualityRationale: Quasi-experiment using intact classroom groups rather than full individual random assignment; a foundational, widely-replicated classroom form-focused-instruction study.

title: Instruction and the Development of Questions in L2 Classrooms
design: Quasi-experimental classroom study with pretest/instructional-treatment/posttest design plus classroom-observation corpus, examining effects of form-focused instruction and corrective feedback on question development
population: Francophone learners aged 10-12 in four intact intensive-ESL classes (grades 5-6) in elementary schools in Quebec, Canada
institution: Concordia University (Lightbown) / OISE, University of Toronto (Spada)
topic: focused L2 instruction and form-focused instruction
outcome: Form-focused instruction and corrective feedback delivered within communicative interaction contributed positively to learners' development of English question forms in both short- and long-term (delayed) posttests.
limitations: Intact, non-randomly-assigned classes showed substantial between-class variability in instructional input, limiting experimental control over the treatment.
qualityRationale: Quasi-experiment with intact classes and a classroom-observation component rather than individual random assignment; a frequently-cited classroom instruction study.

title: Input Enhancement and L2 Question Formation
authors: White, L., Spada, N., Lightbown, P. M., & Ranta, L.
design: Classroom quasi-experiment: three experimental classes received input-enhancement/form-focused instruction on question formation over a two-week period and were compared with an uninstructed control class using pretest, posttest, and delayed-posttest written and oral tasks
population: Beginner-level francophone ESL learners aged 10-12 in classrooms in Quebec, Canada
topic: focused L2 instruction and form-focused instruction
outcome: The instructed group that received input-enhancement activities on question formation made significantly greater gains in accurate question formation than the uninstructed control group on immediate and delayed posttests.
limitations: A small number of intact classes served as the unit of comparison rather than individually randomized learners, and the two-week treatment period limits conclusions about long-term retention.
qualityRationale: Controlled classroom quasi-experiment with an uninstructed comparison group and pre/post/delayed measures, but intact classes rather than individually randomized learners.

title: Corrective Feedback and Learner Uptake: Negotiation of Form in Communicative Classrooms
design: Classroom discourse/observational analysis of naturally occurring teacher corrective feedback and learner uptake, based on audio-recorded and transcribed lessons coded with an error-treatment-sequence model
population: Students in four Grade 4-6 French immersion classrooms in Montreal, Canada, observed across 18.3 hours of classroom interaction spanning 27 lessons (14 subject-matter, 13 French language arts)
outcome: Teachers overwhelmingly favored recasts (about 55% of feedback moves) even though recasts were the feedback type least likely to elicit learner-generated repair; elicitation, metalinguistic feedback, clarification requests, and repetition led to significantly more successful learner repair (uptake).
limitations: Purely observational/correlational classroom design without experimental manipulation of feedback type limits causal claims, and findings come from French immersion content classrooms that may not generalize to other instructional settings.
qualityRationale: Large, seminal, extensively replicated classroom discourse corpus, but observational/descriptive rather than an experimental manipulation of feedback type.

title: One Size Fits All? Recasts, Prompts, and L2 Learning
design: Quasi-experimental classroom study with intact classes assigned to recasts, prompts, or control conditions, using pretest, immediate-posttest, and 4-week-delayed-posttest written and oral measures
population: Grade 6 francophone students in three intact intensive-ESL classes in the Montreal area
institution: Université de Montréal (Ammar) / OISE, University of Toronto (Spada)
outcome: Prompts were overall more effective than recasts for learning third-person possessive determiners (his/her); low-proficiency learners benefited significantly more from prompts than recasts, while high-proficiency learners benefited similarly from both.
limitations: Intact classes rather than individual learners were assigned to conditions, so class-level confounds cannot be ruled out, and only one linguistic target (possessive determiners) was tested.
qualityRationale: Controlled quasi-experiment with pretest/immediate/delayed-posttest design, but conditions were assigned at the intact-class level rather than to individually randomized learners.

title: Input, Interaction, and Second Language Development: An Empirical Study of Question Formation in ESL
design: Controlled experiment with adult learners individually randomly assigned to one of four interaction/feedback conditions or a control group, using pretest, posttest, and delayed-posttest measures of question-form development
population: Adult ESL learners of varying L1 backgrounds in beginner and lower-intermediate intensive English classes at a private language school in Sydney, Australia
outcome: Learners who engaged in interaction involving negotiation and feedback about non-target question forms showed significantly greater developmental progress along the question-formation acquisition sequence than learners who received comprehensible input without interactional feedback.
limitations: Small cell sizes within each of the five groups limit statistical power, and development was measured via movement through developmental stages rather than fine-grained accuracy scores.
qualityRationale: Controlled experiment with individual-level random assignment to five conditions and delayed-posttest measurement, a foundational test of the interaction hypothesis.

title: Learning Simple and Complex Second Language Rules Under Implicit, Incidental, Rule-Search, and Instructed Conditions
design: Randomized controlled laboratory experiment; adult L2 learners individually randomly assigned to implicit, incidental, rule-search, or instructed computerized training conditions for simple and complex grammatical rule sets
population: 104 adult learners of English as a second language
institution: University of Hawai'i at Mānoa (Second Language Teaching & Curriculum Center)
outcome: Explicit instructed conditions produced greater learning than implicit conditions for simple grammatical rules, but implicit and instructed conditions did not differ for complex rules as predicted, only partially supporting claims about implicit-learning advantages for complex material.
limitations: Learning was assessed through a single computerized training/testing paradigm using artificial-feeling sentence stimuli, which may not generalize to naturalistic classroom grammar learning.
qualityRationale: Individually randomized controlled experiment with a sizable sample (N=104) across four learning conditions.

title: The eXperanto Experiment: Effects of Explicit Instruction on Second Language Acquisition
design: Controlled experiment comparing an explicit-instruction group against a group without explicit instruction, both learning four grammatical structures of an artificial language (eXperanto) via computer-controlled self-study, with computerized posttests
population: 54 university students in the Netherlands (27 per group) learning the artificial target language eXperanto
outcome: The explicit-instruction group significantly outperformed the group without explicit instruction on overall L2 grammar acquisition, though the advantage of explicit instruction did not differ significantly by structural complexity or morphology/syntax type.
limitations: The artificial-language (eXperanto) paradigm sacrifices ecological validity for experimental control, so results may not generalize directly to naturalistic classroom acquisition of a real target language.
qualityRationale: Randomized controlled lab experiment with a clear comparison condition, but a moderate sample size (N=54) and an artificial-language paradigm rather than a large multisite/preregistered design.

title: The Effects of Repetition on Vocabulary Knowledge
design: Controlled quasi-experimental study manipulating number of word encounters (1, 3, 7, and 10) in reading passages, using nonsense words substituted for real words in authentic text, assessed with 10 tests covering five aspects of word knowledge (orthography, association, grammatical functions, syntax, meaning and form)
population: 121 Japanese university students learning English as a foreign language
institution: Author affiliation listed as Japan in the publication record
outcome: Greater gains in at least one aspect of word knowledge occurred at each step from 1 to 10 encounters, but no aspect of knowledge was fully mastered even after 10 encounters, indicating more than ten repetitions are likely needed for full word knowledge.
limitations: Use of nonsense words substituted into authentic text may not fully replicate how learners infer meaning from genuine unknown vocabulary in natural reading, limiting ecological validity.
qualityRationale: Well-controlled repeated-measures design with carefully engineered stimuli and multiple knowledge-aspect tests, but a single-population sample, no independent control group, and no random assignment across groups keep it at Grade B.

title: Incidental Vocabulary Acquisition from an Authentic Novel: Do Things Fall Apart?
design: Longitudinal quasi-experiment tracking incidental uptake of 34 low-frequency target words from natural exposure while reading an unmodified authentic novel (Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart) over one month, with pre-, post- and delayed tests of word form and meaning recognition/recall
population: 20 relatively advanced adult EFL learners at a university in Spain
outcome: Learners showed incidental gains in word form and meaning knowledge that scaled with number of exposures in the novel; words met more than 10 times reached about 84% meaning-recognition and 76% spelling-recognition accuracy, while less-frequent words showed much smaller gains.
limitations: Small sample of 20 relatively advanced learners at a single institution limits generalizability, and reading was self-paced and unsupervised outside class, so actual exposure to the text could not be fully controlled.
qualityRationale: Ecologically valid, real incidental-exposure design with delayed testing over a month, but small N=20, a single population/institution, and unsupervised reading limit experimental control.

title: Beyond a Clockwork Orange: Acquiring Second Language Vocabulary Through Reading
authors: Horst, M., Cobb, T., & Meara, P.
design: Quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test study; a complete simplified novel (21,232 words) was read aloud in class over 10 days while students followed along, followed by a 45-item multiple-choice meaning-recognition test and a 13-item word-association test
population: 34 low-intermediate EFL learners in an intensive English program at Sultan Qaboos University, Oman
institution: Concordia University (Horst, Cobb); University of Wales Swansea (Meara)
outcome: Students made significant incidental gains in word meaning recognition and word association after extensive reading of a single simplified novel; learners with larger pre-existing vocabularies made proportionally greater gains, and text word frequency did not reliably predict which words were learned.
limitations: Small single-site sample (34 learners after attrition) reading a single simplified text limits generalizability, and only immediate post-reading vocabulary knowledge was measured, not longer-term retention.
qualityRationale: Classic, widely replicated classroom quasi-experiment with a genuine extensive-reading treatment and real pre/post measurement, but small N and no untreated control condition keep it at Grade B.

title: Maintenance of Foreign Language Vocabulary and the Spacing Effect
authors: Bahrick, H. P., Bahrick, L. E., Bahrick, A. S., & Bahrick, P. E.
design: 9-year longitudinal experiment in which 4 participants learned and relearned 300 English-foreign-language word pairs across 13 or 26 relearning sessions spaced at 14-, 28-, or 56-day intervals, with retention tested 1, 2, 3, or 5 years after training ended
population: 4 members of the Bahrick family (the investigators and their children), the only participants in the study
outcome: Longer intersession spacing slightly slowed initial acquisition but produced substantially higher long-term retention; 13 relearning sessions spaced 56 days apart yielded retention comparable to 26 sessions spaced only 14 days apart, demonstrating a strong spacing effect on foreign-vocabulary maintenance.
limitations: Extremely small, non-random, family-member sample (N=4, including the investigators themselves) severely limits statistical power and generalizability despite the study's unusually long duration.
qualityRationale: Genuine multi-year controlled experiment manipulating spacing interval and session count with real retention data, but the extremely small N=4 family sample precludes an A grade despite the study's rigor and duration.

title: Effects of Expanding and Equal Spacing on Second Language Vocabulary Learning: Does Gradually Increasing Spacing Increase Vocabulary Learning?
design: Controlled factorial lab experiment manipulating spacing type (expanding vs. equal) and amount of spacing (massed, short, medium, long) using flashcard-style retrieval practice on English-Japanese word pairs, with immediate and one-week-delayed posttests
population: 128 Japanese college students studying English as a foreign language
institution: Kansai University, Faculty of Foreign Language Studies
outcome: Spaced practice outperformed massed practice overall, but expanding spacing did not outperform equal spacing; the amount of spacing mattered more than its pattern, with equal spacing at least as effective as expanding spacing for L2 vocabulary retention.
limitations: Learning occurred in a single controlled lab session with decontextualized word pairs rather than authentic classroom input, and retention was measured only up to one week, so longer-term classroom generalizability is untested.
qualityRationale: Large (N=128), fully controlled factorial lab experiment with random assignment to spacing conditions and a delayed posttest, giving strong internal validity.

title: Investigating Distribution of Practice Effects for the Learning of Foreign Language Verb Morphology in the Young Learner Classroom
authors: Kasprowicz, R. E., Marsden, E., & Sephton, N.
design: Cluster classroom quasi-experiment; 8 intact primary-school classes were assigned to different practice schedules (once weekly for 60 minutes vs. twice weekly for 30 minutes) using a computerized grammar game over three weeks to practice French verb inflections, with pre-, post- and delayed tests
population: 113 beginner learners of French aged 8-11 across 8 primary school classes in England
outcome: Distribution of practice (once vs. twice weekly) had little independent effect on learning of French verb morphology; individual differences in language-analytic ability predicted learning gains more strongly than the practice schedule did.
limitations: Classes rather than individual learners were the unit of assignment (cluster design), and only two distribution schedules over a short three-week period were compared, limiting power to detect smaller spacing effects.
qualityRationale: Real classroom cluster-controlled study with over 100 young learners across 8 classes, a genuine comparison of practice schedules, and pre/post/delayed measurement; won Best of MLJ 2019.

title: Fluency Training in the ESL Classroom: An Experimental Study of Fluency Development and Proceduralization
authors: de Jong, N., & Perfetti, C. A.
design: Classroom experiment; students completed three training sessions recording timed speeches (4, 3, 2 minutes), with one group repeating the same topic across sessions and another group speaking on three different topics, followed by fluency posttests on novel topics
population: 24 students enrolled in English-as-a-second-language classes
institution: Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam (de Jong); University of Pittsburgh (Perfetti)
outcome: Fluency improved during training for both groups, but only the group that repeated the same topic maintained fluency gains on a later posttest with new topics; these learners reused more non-topic-specific words/phrases across repetitions, supporting a proceduralization account of fluency development.
limitations: Very small sample (N=24) split across two conditions limits statistical power, and the narrow set of topics/task types used limits generalization to broader classroom speaking tasks.
qualityRationale: Controlled experiment with a genuine comparison condition (same-topic vs. different-topic repetition) and objective fluency measures, but a small sample (N=24) limits it to Grade B.

title: The Effects of Task Repetition on Linguistic Output
authors: Gass, S., Mackey, A., Alvarez-Torres, M. J., & Fernández-García, M.
design: Controlled experiment with a repeated-task group (watched and orally narrated in Spanish the same video three times, then a new video), a varied-task group (different videos each time), and a control group (video only at Time 1 and Time 4); narrations analyzed for overall proficiency, morphosyntax, and lexical sophistication
population: 84 upper-intermediate university learners of Spanish as a second language
outcome: Task repetition led to improved overall proficiency, selected morphosyntactic accuracy, and lexical sophistication in oral output for the group that repeated the same task, but there was no significant carryover of these gains when learners then performed a new, unpracticed task.
limitations: The task was a narrow narrative video-description task, and repetition benefits did not transfer to a new task, so findings may not generalize to other task types or longer-term retention of gains.
qualityRationale: Foundational controlled experiment with a genuine control group and 84 participants across repeated/varied/control conditions, but a single task type and no delayed posttest keep it at Grade B rather than A.

title: Task Repetition and Second Language Speech Processing
authors: Lambert, C., Kormos, J., & Minn, D.
design: Within-subjects experiment; 32 learners at three proficiency levels performed three oral communication task types (instruction, narration, opinion) six times each (procedural task repetition), with speech rate, filled pauses, and self-repairs analyzed as fluency measures tied to stages of speech production
population: 32 Japanese learners of English sampled at three proficiency levels
outcome: Repeated performance of the same task type increased speech rate and reduced clause-final and mid-clause filled pauses across repetitions, with patterns differing by proficiency level and task type, indicating repetition eases specific stages of L2 speech processing (conceptualization, formulation, monitoring) rather than uniformly boosting fluency.
limitations: Small sample (N=32) split across three proficiency levels and three task types yields small per-cell sizes, and all learners shared a single L1/national background, limiting generalizability.
qualityRationale: Controlled within-subjects design with objective speech-processing measures across repeated performances, but a modest sample (N=32) spread across proficiency and task-type cells limits it to Grade B.

title: Effects of Negotiation on Language Learners' Output
design: Classroom quasi-experiment comparing child dyads who negotiated for meaning during a picture-description task against dyads who did not negotiate
population: 48 fifth-grade native and non-native speakers of Dutch in a Flemish primary school in Belgium
institution: University of Leuven (Centre for Language and Education)
outcome: Children who were pushed to negotiate meaning subsequently produced a greater quantity of output, conveyed more essential task information, and used a wider range of vocabulary than children who had not negotiated, though negotiation did not improve grammatical accuracy or syntactic complexity.
limitations: The study measured only output on an immediate follow-up task, so it cannot speak to durable long-term acquisition, and the child sample was drawn from one school system.
qualityRationale: Controlled comparison of negotiation vs. non-negotiation conditions in an intact classroom sample, but not randomized at the individual level and moderate sample size.

title: Input, Interaction, and Second Language Production
authors: Gass, S. M., & Varonis, E. M.
design: Controlled laboratory experiment using a two-way direction-giving task comparing modified-input-only, interaction-only, both, and neither conditions across native-nonnative speaker dyads
population: 16 native speaker-nonnative speaker dyads of adult ESL learners
outcome: Both modified input and interaction independently improved nonnative speakers' immediate task comprehension, but only interaction (negotiation of meaning) carried over to improve performance on a subsequent, similar task, indicating interaction had a longer-lasting effect than input modification alone.
limitations: The very small sample of 16 dyads and single task type (direction-giving) limit statistical power and generalizability to other task types or proficiency levels.
qualityRationale: Controlled lab experiment with a factorial comparison of input/interaction conditions, but a very small dyad sample.

title: Comprehensible Input and Second Language Acquisition: What Is the Relationship?
design: Controlled experiment assigning learners to unmodified input with no interaction, premodified input with no interaction, or unmodified input with negotiated interaction
population: 41 beginning-level learners of Japanese as a second language
outcome: The negotiated-interaction group showed the highest comprehension of the input, and learners who heard premodified or interactionally modified input showed some vocabulary gains, but interactional modification did not produce a clear acquisition advantage for the target Japanese locative structures over the other conditions.
limitations: The study used a short, single-session treatment and a modest sample per condition, so it cannot establish whether comprehension advantages translate into durable long-term acquisition.
qualityRationale: Controlled three-group experiment with assignment to distinct input/interaction conditions, but a single short session and modest per-group sample size.

title: Problems in Output and the Cognitive Processes They Generate: A Step Towards Second Language Learning
design: Descriptive/exploratory study using think-aloud protocols during a written composition task, followed by qualitative coding of learners' language-related episodes
population: 18 grade 8 early French immersion students in Ontario, Canada
institution: Ontario Institute for Studies in Education, University of Toronto
outcome: While producing output under a role-play writing task, students noticed and consciously responded to language problems an average of just over ten times each, using their existing linguistic knowledge to test and revise hypotheses about the language, supporting output's proposed noticing and hypothesis-testing functions in L2 learning.
limitations: The design had no comparison group and relied on think-aloud verbal reports, which can alter task performance and cannot fully capture unconscious processing.
qualityRationale: Controlled, systematic classroom task with a defined coding scheme applied to verbal-report data, but a small sample and no control/comparison group.

title: Classroom Interaction, Comprehension, and the Acquisition of L2 Word Meanings
authors: Ellis, R., Tanaka, Y., & Yamazaki, A.
design: Two linked classroom quasi-experiments comparing interactionally modified input against premodified (simplified, non-interactive) input for listening comprehension and incidental vocabulary acquisition
population: Japanese high school EFL students across two classroom studies (79 learners in Study 1 and 127 learners in Study 2)
outcome: Across both studies, students who received interactionally modified input comprehended the listening passage better and acquired a greater number of new vocabulary word meanings than students who received premodified input, showing an advantage for interactionally negotiated input over simplified but non-interactive input.
limitations: Classes were intact, pre-existing groups rather than randomly assigned individuals, and vocabulary acquisition was measured immediately rather than at a later delayed interval.
qualityRationale: Two-study replication design with a controlled input-condition comparison and a reasonably large combined sample, but intact classroom groups rather than individual random assignment.

title: Task Difficulty in Oral Speech Act Production
design: Controlled experiment comparing native speakers and two L2 proficiency groups on oral role-play production of requests and refusals across low- and high-difficulty (power/distance/imposition) situations
population: 20 native English speakers and 59 Japanese learners of English (lower- and higher-proficiency EFL learners) at a Japanese university
outcome: L2 learners produced low-imposition/low-power-difference speech acts significantly faster and more appropriately than high-difficulty ones, and proficiency significantly affected appropriateness ratings and speech rate, while native speakers showed little difference across difficulty levels, showing that pragmatic task difficulty affects L2 but not native-speaker production.
limitations: The task situations were limited to requests and refusals in a role-play format, so findings may not generalize to other speech acts or to spontaneous, unscripted interaction.
qualityRationale: Controlled comparison across proficiency groups and a native-speaker baseline with a systematically manipulated task variable, but a single-site sample and role-play elicitation rather than naturalistic interaction.

title: Negative Feedback as Regulation and Second Language Learning in the Zone of Proximal Development
design: Longitudinal qualitative case study analyzing tutor-learner dialogic mediation across weekly one-on-one writing tutorial sessions over a semester
population: 3 adult ESL learners and their tutor in one-on-one writing tutorials at a U.S. university
outcome: As tutoring progressed, the graduated, negotiated feedback the tutor provided (a regulatory scale from implicit to explicit mediation) became progressively more implicit for each learner, and learners required decreasing amounts of tutor mediation to self-correct errors, consistent with movement toward self-regulation within the zone of proximal development.
limitations: The extremely small sample (3 learners) and single-tutor design mean findings are illustrative rather than statistically generalizable, and there was no comparison group receiving non-graduated feedback.
qualityRationale: Systematic longitudinal case-study design with a coded regulatory scale applied consistently across sessions, but an extremely small N and no control condition.

title: Accent, Intelligibility, and Comprehensibility: Evidence from Four L1s
authors: Derwing, T. M., & Munro, M. J.
design: Cross-sectional rating study: recorded L2 speech samples were rated and transcribed by native-speaker listeners for accentedness, comprehensibility, and intelligibility
population: 48 intermediate-proficiency ESL learners (12 each from Cantonese, Japanese, Polish, and Spanish L1 backgrounds) recorded in Canada; their speech was rated by a panel of 26 native English-speaking listeners
institution: University of Alberta; Simon Fraser University
outcome: Accentedness, comprehensibility, and intelligibility were found to be partially independent dimensions of L2 speech: a speaker could be heavily accented yet still highly intelligible and comprehensible, and the linguistic factors contributing to each dimension differed.
limitations: The sample was restricted to intermediate-proficiency learners from four L1 backgrounds rated by a single regional (Canadian) listener panel, limiting generalization to other proficiency levels and listener populations.
qualityRationale: Well-controlled rating study with a real listener panel and balanced L1 groups, but a single-site convenience sample without random assignment or a preregistered design.

title: Learning Second Language Suprasegmentals: Effect of L2 Experience on Prosody and Fluency Characteristics of L2 Speech
design: Cross-sectional quasi-experiment comparing three L2-experience groups (3 months, 3 years, 10 years of U.S. residence) plus a native-speaker control group on acoustic production and native-listener ratings of five suprasegmentals
population: 30 adult Korean learners of English (10 each at 3 months, 3 years, and 10 years of U.S. residence) and 10 adult native English speaker controls
outcome: Length of L2 experience predicted improvement in stress timing, while age of arrival (rather than experience per se) predicted speech rate, pause frequency, and pause duration; suprasegmentals contributed to perceived foreign accent at every experience level.
limitations: The design was cross-sectional rather than longitudinal, so individual developmental trajectories could not be tracked, and the sample was limited to one L1 (Korean) group in one host-country context.
qualityRationale: Controlled comparison across three well-defined experience groups plus native-speaker controls with both acoustic and perceptual measures, but cross-sectional, single-L1, and modest per-cell sample sizes (n=10).

title: Age Effects on Late Bilingualism: The Production Development of /r/ by High-Proficiency Japanese Learners of English
design: Cross-sectional group-comparison study of L2 phoneme production, comparing late bilinguals with varying ages of acquisition against native-speaker and low-proficiency comparison groups using acoustic and rated production measures
population: 88 late Japanese-English bilinguals (age of acquisition >16 years) plus comparison groups of 10 native English speakers and 10 low-proficiency Japanese learners of English
outcome: Age of acquisition significantly predicted attained accuracy of English /r/ production at a spontaneous (picture description) speech level but not at a controlled (word/sentence reading) level, indicating age effects depend on speech task demands.
limitations: The design was cross-sectional and correlational rather than a true experiment, so causal claims about age of acquisition are limited, and results are specific to one L1-L2 pairing (Japanese-English) and one phoneme.
qualityRationale: Large, well-controlled cross-sectional sample (N=108) with matched comparison groups and multiple speech-elicitation tasks, but a correlational (non-experimental) design without random assignment to age-of-acquisition conditions.

title: Orchestrating Strategy Use: Toward a Model of the Skilled Second Language Listener
design: Descriptive/correlational study using coded think-aloud protocols to compare listening-strategy use between more-skilled and less-skilled L2 listeners
population: 36 Grade 7 students learning French as a second language in Canadian classrooms
outcome: More-skilled listeners used metacognitive strategies (planning, monitoring, evaluating, problem-solving) in a more orchestrated, purposeful way than less-skilled listeners, who applied strategies more sporadically and with less overall coordination.
limitations: The study relied on think-aloud self-report data from a single age/grade cohort learning one target language, which may not generalize to other learner populations or listening contexts.
qualityRationale: Careful mixed qualitative-quantitative design with coded think-aloud protocols, but a small single-cohort sample and no experimental manipulation limit generalizability.

title: Teaching L2 Learners How to Listen Does Make a Difference: An Empirical Study
design: Quasi-experimental classroom intervention across a semester comparing a metacognitive process-based listening pedagogy (experimental group) to a same-materials comparison condition (control group) in intact class sections
population: 106 university students in six intact sections of French-as-a-second-language courses (59 in the metacognitive-instruction group, 47 in the control group), taught by the same teacher
outcome: The metacognitive-instruction group showed significantly greater gains in listening comprehension over the semester than the control group, and the performance gap between less-skilled and more-skilled listeners narrowed in the experimental group.
limitations: Assignment was by intact class section rather than individual random assignment, so section-level confounds cannot be fully ruled out despite using the same teacher across all sections.
qualityRationale: A genuine semester-long controlled classroom intervention with a comparison condition, pre/post measures, and a reasonably large combined sample (N=106), but assignment was by class section rather than full individual randomization.

title: Suprasegmental Measures of Accentedness and Judgments of Language Learner Proficiency in Oral English
authors: Kang, O., Rubin, D., & Pickering, L.
design: Validity study combining instrumental acoustic analysis of suprasegmental features with a rating experiment in which naive listeners judged recorded speech samples for oral proficiency and comprehensibility
population: 26 speech samples from iBT TOEFL examinees (Chinese, Spanish, Korean, and Arabic L1 backgrounds) judged by 188 monolingual U.S. undergraduate listener-raters
institution: Northern Arizona University; University of Georgia; Georgia State University
outcome: Instrumentally measured suprasegmental features (speech rate, pause, and intonation measures) collectively accounted for about 50% of the variance in listeners' oral-proficiency and comprehensibility ratings, showing that acoustic accentedness measures are strongly associated with the listener judgments underlying oral-proficiency assessment.
limitations: Raters were monolingual U.S. undergraduates rather than trained certified examiners, and the speech samples were limited to four L1 groups from one test-taking context, limiting generalization to other rater populations and assessment formats.
qualityRationale: A well-powered rating experiment (188 raters) combined with objective acoustic measurement, but the rater sample was a single convenience population of undergraduates rather than trained assessment raters, and it is not a randomized or preregistered design.

title: Relationship of TOEFL iBT Scores to Academic Performance: Some Evidence from American Universities
design: Large-scale multi-institution predictive-validity study relating standardized test scores to subsequent academic outcomes (GPA), using regression and expectancy-table analyses across student subgroups
population: 2,594 undergraduate and graduate international students at 10 American universities, with TOEFL iBT, GRE, GMAT, and/or SAT scores linked to their academic records
outcome: TOEFL iBT scores significantly predicted subsequent GPA (explaining roughly 6-7% of variance alone), with predictive validity broadly comparable across subgroups but somewhat stronger for business/humanities/social-science majors than for science/engineering majors.
limitations: The study is correlational with no experimental manipulation of test scores or instruction, relies on self-selected students who were admitted and enrolled, and predictive power for GPA alone was modest even where statistically significant.
qualityRationale: Large multisite sample (N=2,594 across 10 universities) with real institutional academic-record data, multiple predictor controls, and subgroup analyses gives strong evidential weight, even though the design remains observational rather than experimental.

title: Age Constraints on Second-Language Acquisition
authors: Flege, J. E., Yeni-Komshian, G. H., & Liu, S.
design: Cross-sectional study testing the critical period hypothesis by relating age of arrival to L2 pronunciation (foreign-accent ratings) and morphosyntax (grammaticality judgment) scores across a wide age-of-arrival range
population: 240 native Korean speakers residing in the United States, spanning ages of arrival from 1 to 23 years and a mean length of residence of about 15 years
outcome: As age of arrival increased, foreign-accent ratings grew stronger and grammaticality-judgment scores decreased steadily and roughly linearly, with no sharp discontinuity at a single critical-period cutoff.
limitations: The design was cross-sectional rather than longitudinal, and length-of-residence, education, and language-use variables that correlate with age of arrival could not be fully disentangled from age effects themselves.
qualityRationale: A large, carefully designed cross-sectional sample (N=240) spanning a wide continuous range of age of arrival with two independent outcome measures, but it is a single-site, non-experimental design without random assignment or multisite replication.

title: The Robustness of Critical Period Effects in Second Language Acquisition
design: Cross-sectional study testing the Fundamental Difference Hypothesis by relating age of arrival and measured verbal analytical ability to performance on a grammaticality judgment test
population: 57 adult Hungarian-speaking immigrants to the United States who arrived at varying ages
outcome: Very few post-childhood arrivals scored within the range typical of child arrivals on the grammaticality judgment test, and the few adults who did so had high verbal analytical ability, suggesting age-related constraints that may be partly offset by analytical aptitude in adulthood.
limitations: The sample was limited to one L1 group (Hungarian) with a modest overall N, and grammaticality judgment is only one measure of ultimate L2 attainment, limiting generalization to other skills or populations.
qualityRationale: Controlled comparison relating age of arrival and a measured aptitude variable to a validated grammaticality judgment test, but a single-L1 sample of modest size without random assignment or a fully continuous age design.

title: The Subtle Effects of Language Anxiety on Cognitive Processing in the Second Language
authors: MacIntyre, P. D., & Gardner, R. C.
design: Experimental study measuring language anxiety and assessing cognitive processing at three stages (input, processing, output) using timed L2 tasks
population: 97 college students enrolled in French-as-a-second-language courses
outcome: Language anxiety was significantly related to performance at each of the input, processing, and output stages of L2 cognitive processing, with more anxious students showing poorer performance across stages.
limitations: Participants were university French learners at a single institution, and anxiety was assessed via self-report questionnaires rather than physiological or behavioral measures, limiting generalization across contexts and target languages.
qualityRationale: A well-designed multi-stage experimental task with a reasonably sized sample (N=97) and validated anxiety measures, but single-institution, single-target-language sampling limits external validity.

title: The Two Faces of Janus? Anxiety and Enjoyment in the Foreign Language Classroom
design: Large-scale cross-sectional survey study correlating Foreign Language Enjoyment (FLE) and Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety (FLCA) scale scores with learner background variables
population: 1,746 foreign language learners from around the world, surveyed online across a range of ages, proficiency levels, and target languages
venue: Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching
institution: Birkbeck, University of London; Cape Breton University
outcome: Foreign Language Enjoyment scores were significantly higher than Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety scores overall, and both FLE and FLCA were significantly linked to variables including perceived relative proficiency, number of languages known, and gender.
limitations: The design was cross-sectional and relied entirely on self-report survey measures collected via convenience/snowball sampling online, so causal direction between enjoyment/anxiety and the correlated variables cannot be established.
qualityRationale: A very large international convenience sample (N=1,746) strengthens the survey's descriptive power, but the design is a purely observational, self-report cross-sectional survey without random sampling or experimental controls.
